narration: Welcome back. This lecture is why machines need controllers.
By the end, you will be able to explain what a P L C does, and where it sits between the field devices and the operator.
We will look at relay logic, meet the motor starter bench, and see where PLCs are used across South African mines, factories and water works.
Walk onto the floor of almost any mine, factory or water works in South Africa, and you will find machines that start, stop and protect themselves automatically.
Decades ago, that automatic behaviour came from relay logic. Rooms full of wired relays, each one doing a single job.
Relay panels work, but they are slow to change. To alter one step, someone has to rewire it.
Today, almost all of that relay logic has moved into a single small computer, the programmable logic controller, or P L C.
One P L C can replace a whole relay room, and its logic can be changed in software, not with a screwdriver.
So what does a P L C actually do.
It sits between the field devices and the operator.
On one side, field devices. Push buttons, limit switches, sensors. These send signals in.
The P L C reads those signals as inputs.
Inside the P L C, a program decides what should happen. This is the C P U, the central processing unit.
On the other side, the P L C writes outputs. It switches contactors, lamps and valves.
The operator watches and controls all of this from a panel or a screen, without ever touching the wiring.
Let's meet the machine we will use throughout Stage One, the motor starter bench.
Here is the Start button and the Stop button, the field devices an operator presses.
Here is the contactor, the switch that actually turns the motor on.
And here is the motor itself, the machine doing the work.
Between the buttons and the motor sits the P L C. It reads the buttons as inputs, and drives the contactor as an output.
Every machine in this course works the same way. Inputs in, logic in the middle, outputs out.
Later in this stage, you will program this bench yourself, in ladder logic.
You will see the same logic on two real controller families.
On a Siemens S seven twelve hundred, inputs and outputs are addressed like I zero point zero, and Q zero point zero.
On an Allen Bradley CompactLogix, the same signals get named tags, like Start button.
Different brands, same idea. Inputs come in, logic runs, outputs go out.
So, a P L C reads inputs from field devices, runs a program, and writes outputs, the same way relay logic always has, just faster, and far easier to change.
For your lab, go to the motor starter bench, and name every part. Say whether each one is an input or an output.
Get comfortable with that one idea, inputs and outputs, because every lecture from here builds on it.
One last thing.
This is simulated training. It builds real skill, but it is not permission to work on live plant. Always follow your site's rules, and work under supervision.
Up next, module one continues with inside the P L C, C P U, power and I O.
I will see you there.
